newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew prepare for homecoming.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew prepare for homecoming.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Discovery were packing up their gear on Sunday and preparing to return to Earth after a successful 11-day research mission.
The $2 billion reusable spaceship was due to touch down at NASA's Kennedy Space Center on Monday, at 7:14 a.m. EDT (1114 GMT), 20 minutes after sunrise.
Discovery, reentering the atmosphere over the South Pacific, will make a rare southerly approach to the Florida peninsula that will take it over Central America and close to the shoreline of Cuba.
Although the weather is expected to be "excellent" for the shuttle's homecoming, forecasters were keeping a close eye on conditions at the Florida spaceport.
"The weather is never without surprises," flight director Wayne Hale told a news conference.
The shuttle's alternative landing strip in California was not being considered for Monday, he said.
Discovery has only one daylight landing opportunity at each of its runways because NASA wants to avoid a more risky predawn touchdown. Usually there are two landing slots available at each site.
The shuttle has enough fuel and supplies to stay in orbit until Thursday, Hale said.

During their final day aloft, Discovery's crew tested a robot arm positioning system needed for the assembly of the planned international space station and lowered the shuttle's orbit from 185 miles (297 km) to 160 miles (257 km) for some last-minute atmospheric studies.
Although the mission lacked the glamor of a Mir docking or a Hubble repair, it was a major step forward in preparing for the start of space station construction next year, Hale said.
"It looks like we are going to get a 100 or maybe more than 100 percent of all the objectives for each and every payload we flew," he said.
Scientists at the Kennedy Space Center were eagerly awaiting the bounty of ozone data stored aboard the atmospheric satellite retrieved by Discovery on Saturday.
The spacecraft, which flew free of the shuttle for nine days, made nearly 50,000 atmospheric measurements.
